runbook:
Weekly security update report. Investigate only and change nothing: never install, upgrade, refresh package lists or reboot. Every command must be read-only; anything else is refused.

Check every target host. The fleet may have over 50 hosts, so keep each call small: send each command to every host of a family in one run_command call, except where a step says to batch. Start with get_host_facts and sort hosts into the Debian family (Debian, Ubuntu) and the RHEL family (RHEL, Rocky, Alma, CentOS Stream, Fedora, Oracle Linux, Amazon Linux). Note any other system as not checked.

1. RHEL family, pending advisories: `dnf updateinfo summary` (or `yum updateinfo summary` where dnf is missing) gives the counts by severity (Critical, Important, Moderate, Low) and the bugfix and enhancement counts in a few lines. On hosts with Critical or Important advisories only, at most 10 hosts per call, list them with `dnf updateinfo list --security --sec-severity Critical` and the same for Important; if dnf refuses --sec-severity, keep the summary.
2. Debian family, pending updates: `apt list --upgradable`, at most 10 hosts per call, since it prints one line per package. A package is a security update when its suite contains `-security` (for example `bookworm-security`, `noble-security`, `noble-infra-security`). Count total and security updates per host, and name up to five security packages, preferring the kernel, openssl, openssh, libc, sudo and systemd. Debian and Ubuntu give no severity here: list their security updates without a level. If the output was cut, give the count as at least what you saw, marked with >.
3. Reboot required:
   - Debian family: `cat /var/run/reboot-required.pkgs` names the packages that need it. Where the file does not exist, `test -f /var/run/reboot-required` (exit code 0 means a reboot is needed, packages unknown; 1 means none).
   - RHEL family: `dnf needs-restarting -r` (exit code 1 means a reboot is needed and it names the packages, 0 means none). Where it is not available, say unknown.
   - All hosts: `uname -r` and `find /boot -maxdepth 1 -name 'vmlinuz-*'`. When the newest installed kernel is newer than the running one, a reboot is pending even if nothing else says so.
4. Last update, all hosts in one call: `stat -L -c '%y %n' /var/lib/dpkg/status /var/cache/apt/pkgcache.bin /var/lib/rpm/rpmdb.sqlite /var/lib/rpm/Packages /usr/lib/sysimage/rpm/rpmdb.sqlite`. Each host has only some of these files; ignore the errors for the others. The dpkg status file or the rpm database changed last when packages were last installed or upgraded; pkgcache.bin is when apt last refreshed its package lists. Give both in days before this run. When the lists are older than 7 days, the Debian family counts may miss updates; say so.
5. If a command is refused, fails for lack of permission or times out, note the check as not run on that host and move on; do not work around it.

Severity of a host: critical with a pending Critical advisory, or with pending security updates and a last update more than 30 days ago; warning with any other pending security update or a pending reboot; info otherwise. The report takes the worst host's severity.

In the report, put one Markdown table for the whole fleet under Evidence, one row per host with anything pending, sorted by severity and then host name, with the columns: Host, OS, Security (counts by severity on the RHEL family, a count on the Debian family), Other updates, Reboot (with the packages that need it), Kernel (running and newest installed), Last update (days), List age (days, Debian family). Name the hosts with nothing pending on one line after the table, and the hosts not checked on another, with the reason. Under Recommendations, name the hosts to patch first and those to reboot, briefly.
